Scheduled Runs & Crons ​

A cron is a small durable record that says: at this schedule, start a Run with this brief. That is the whole of it. A cron owns no execution machinery — firing calls the run engine's startRun(), so a scheduled task gets everything a Run already has: PRIME orchestration, a shared context, approval gates, notifications, and a thread you can open and steer.

The trade this makes is deliberate. There is no queue, no worker pool, and no separate scheduled-job runtime to reason about. There is a clock, and there are runs.

The cron record ​

ts
interface CronJob {
  id: string;
  orgId?: string;
  createdBy?: string;
  name: string;
  schedule: string;
  brief: string;
  project?: string;
  enabled: boolean;
  createdAt: number;
  updatedAt: number;
  nextFireAt?: number;
  lastFiredAt?: number;
  lastRunId?: string;
  lastSkippedAt?: number;
  lastSkipReason?: string;
}
FieldPurpose
idGenerated at creation; also the Mongo _id
orgIdOwning org in cloud mode. Absent on local records, which resolve to local
createdByFires act as this user — their budget, effort ceiling, and agent access govern the fired run
nameShort human label, and the fired run's title
scheduleThe cron expression, evaluated in local time
briefThe objective handed to startRun() on every fire
projectOptional registry project the fired run is scoped to
enabledThe kill switch
nextFireAtNext occurrence, ms epoch. Recomputed on boot, after every fire, and after every edit
lastFiredAtWhen the last successful fire happened
lastRunIdThe run created by the most recent fire — the only link between a cron and its runs
lastSkippedAt / lastSkipReasonWhy the most recent attempt did not produce a run

There is no field pointing from a run back to the cron that started it. The relationship is one-directional: the cron remembers its lastRunId.

Schedule syntax ​

Schedules are parsed by croner, which accepts the standard five-field expression plus an optional leading seconds field and an optional trailing year field:

┌───────────── (optional) second   0-59
│ ┌─────────── minute              0-59
│ │ ┌───────── hour                0-23
│ │ │ ┌─────── day of month        1-31
│ │ │ │ ┌───── month               1-12 or JAN-DEC
│ │ │ │ │ ┌─── day of week         0-7 or SUN-SAT
│ │ │ │ │ │
* * * * * *

Beyond the usual *, ,, -, and /, croner supports L (last), W (nearest weekday), and # (nth weekday of the month).

ExpressionFires
0 9 * * 1-5Weekdays at 09:00
*/30 * * * *Every 30 minutes
0 7 1 * *07:00 on the first of each month
0 18 * * FRIFridays at 18:00

Sub-minute precision is not useful in practice. The scheduler sweeps on a timer whose default is 60 seconds, so an expression finer than that fires at most once per sweep.

A schedule is validated before it is stored, by asking croner for the next occurrence. An expression that fails to parse, or that parses but never fires, is rejected with the parser's own message rather than being silently accepted.

Timezone ​

Croner is constructed with no timezone option, so every schedule is evaluated in the host process's local time — whatever TZ or system zone the server runs under. There is no per-cron timezone field on the record, in the Mongo schema, or in the create/update path.

In a multi-tenant deployment this means all orgs' crons fire on the server's clock, not on each member's. If your members are not in the server's zone, write the expression in the server's zone.

What a fire does ​

fireCron() wraps everything in the cron's own tenant scope — its orgId, acting as its createdBy user, with via: 'cron' — and then calls the run engine directly:

ts
const run = await startRun({
  brief: c.brief,
  project: c.project,
  title: c.name,
  playbookId: playbookForBrief(c.brief),
});

That last argument matters. A cron is by definition repeated work, so if a playbook was already proven and saved for this exact brief, the fire replays it rather than paying to re-derive a plan — and lands on the same shape of result every time instead of a fresh interpretation.

Nothing else is passed. Effort mode, provider profile, model, and execution mode all fall back to the Settings defaults in force at the moment of the fire, and are then stamped onto the run so a later Settings change cannot reshape work already in flight.

startRun() applies its normal gates regardless of who called it: the credit hard stop, org status, the member's monthly budget, and the member's and org's live-run concurrency ceilings. A cron fire that trips one of these throws, and is recorded as a skip.

On success the cron stamps lastFiredAt and lastRunId, clears any previous skip fields, and is persisted.

Overlap ​

Overlapping fires are skipped, not queued. Before firing, the scheduler checks whether the run from the previous fire is still live:

A schedule's previous run counts as still live when its status is active orawaiting_input. If it is, this fire is dropped.

Note that awaiting_input counts as live. A run blocked on a question or an approval gate holds the slot — a daily cron whose run is sitting on an unanswered approval will keep skipping until you answer it. That is the intended behaviour: double-booking the same project with two runs working the same brief is worse than a missed day.

A skipped fire records lastSkippedAt and a lastSkipReason naming the run that blocked it, then rolls nextFireAt forward to the next occurrence.

The same check runs inside fireCron() itself, so the manual "run now" path refuses too, with a 409.

There is no distributed lock or leader election. The scheduler is an in-process timer, so two orchestrator processes sharing one database would each sweep the same crons.

Failure behaviour ​

A cron is never auto-disabled. There is no failure counter, no retry, and no lastError field on the record.

If startRun() throws, the error message is written to lastSkipReason with lastSkippedAt, nextFireAt rolls forward, and the cron tries again at its next occurrence. A genuine failure and an overlap skip therefore surface through the same two fields — read the reason text to tell them apart.

One edge worth knowing: if a schedule somehow becomes unparseable, nextFireAt is cleared, the sweep's self-heal branch tries to recompute it every tick, and the cron stays enabled but never fires. Nothing surfaces as an error. Validation on create and update is what normally prevents this.

Enable, disable, and edit ​

enabled: false is a pause, not a delete. A disabled cron keeps its record and its history but has its nextFireAt cleared, and the sweep skips it entirely.

Any edit re-anchors the schedule from now. Change the brief, the name, the project, or the schedule itself and nextFireAt is recomputed from the current moment — so an edit at 14:00 to a 0 9 * * * cron sets the next fire to tomorrow morning, never to a moment that has already passed. Re-enabling a paused cron does the same.

Deleting a cron is permanent and stops future fires. Runs it already started are unaffected and continue normally.

The sweep ​

startCronScheduler() is called once at startup, after the org stores are hydrated and after the run engine is configured — the scheduler starts runs, so the engine must be ready before it ticks.

The boot pass recomputes every enabled cron's nextFireAt from now. This is the missed-fires-are-skipped policy: occurrences that passed while the server was off or asleep never fire, and nothing catches up on restart.

Then a self-rescheduling setTimeout — not a setInterval — sweeps every loaded org, each inside its own tenant scope. Using a fresh timeout each pass means a change to cronTickSeconds in Settings applies from the next sweep with no restart. The timer is unrefed, so it never keeps the process alive on its own.

SettingDefaultNotes
cronTickSeconds60Sweep interval. Minimum 5; values below that are rejected

Each sweep, per org: bail immediately if no cron is enabled; then for each enabled cron, self-heal a missing nextFireAt, skip anything not yet due, and otherwise either skip for overlap or fire. See Settings.

Where state lives ​

MongoDB is authoritative. Each cron is one document keyed by its own id, written with a full replacement rather than a patch, so cleared optional fields such as lastSkipReason actually disappear instead of lingering.

In memory, each org has a CronStore holding the working copy — the same working-copy plus write-through shape the run store uses. memory/crons.json exists only as legacy migration input; in cloud mode the store refuses to persist at all while Mongo is unavailable, rather than silently writing to a file nobody reads.

Every durable change is broadcast to that org's dashboards over the WebSocket bridge as cron_update, and a deletion as cron_removed. Crons have no streaming — there is nothing to stream, since the work itself happens inside the run.

Managing crons ​

Over HTTP:

MethodPathPurpose
GET/api/cronsList, most recently updated first
POST/api/cronsCreate { name, schedule, brief, project?, enabled? }
PATCH/api/crons/:idUpdate any of the same fields
DELETE/api/crons/:idPermanently delete
POST/api/crons/:id/runFire now — still refuses with 409 if the previous run is live

Or in chat, through PRIME's tools — list_crons, create_cron, update_cron, and delete_cron, all gated on the crons.manage permission, with deletion asking you to confirm first:

create_cron(
  name: "Morning triage",
  schedule: "0 9 * * 1-5",
  brief: "Review overnight alerts and open a summary.",
  project: "billing-api"
)

Both paths run through the same validation module, so a schedule PRIME accepts is exactly one the API would accept.

Crons versus reflexes ​

The two automations are deliberately symmetrical: a reflex is a cron whose trigger is an event instead of a clock. They share the convention of acting as their creator and of starting runs, but they are separate subsystems.

CronReflex
TriggerA scheduleA matched event on the bus
ActionAlways: start a runOne of several action kinds
Controlsenabledenabled, cooldownSec, dedupKey, maxFires, requireApproval
Auto-disableNeverAfter maxFires
Repeat suppressionOverlap skipCooldown and dedup key
HistoryLast fire and last skip onlyA full append-only fire log

A cron does not emit an event, and cron is not an event source — so a reflex cannot be made to listen for a cron firing. If you need that chain, have the cron's run finish and match on the resulting run.finished event instead.
